newsitem.title: LEBANON: Bank of Lebanon limits t-bill issue.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Lebanon limits t-bill issue.

text.p: The Bank of Lebanon has begun limiting the amount of treasury bills it issues to individuals and foreign-based institutions for the first time, Beirut market sources said on Monday.

At Saturday's auction of three- and six-month bills, the bank restricted amounts awarded to non-competitive bids, those made by private individuals and foreign-based institutions, to 10 percent and 14 percent, respectively, the sources said.
"They surprised the market on Saturday. For the first time in the history of Lebanon they refused to give more than a percentage of the non-competitive bids," a dealer told Reuters.
"It means there will be a very good premium on treasury bills," he said.

Earlier this month, the central bank began reporting the percentages it awards of competitive bids, or those from Lebanese banks and financial institutions, which are small percentages of the bids made.
Bankers told Reuters they were awaiting results of Monday's auction of 12- and 24-month bills to seeif their sales to non-competitive bidders would also be limited.
But one banker said the central bank's action on Saturday signalled the end of the recent drop in interest rates on Lebanese pound-denominated t-bills was in sight.
He said the bank believed rates were approaching the right level after having dropped in recent months at a faster pace than the market had expected.
"The monetary authorities don't want to witness a sharper decrease in interest rates," the banker told Reuters.
"This is why they have begun accepting percentages of non-competitive as well as competitive bids.
"They feel that interest rates are approaching the bottom. The return on the Lebanese pound should be more or less on this level," he added.
"The issue is not to reach too low interest rates, which would make the Lebanese pound less interesting to investors."

T-bills are the government's main source for funding Lebanon's swelling public debt. High interest rates in recent years have made them popular but have raised the cost of servicing the debt while the government is under pressure from parliament to curb its growth.
Yields on t-bills currently range from 13.87-16.18 percent compared with 14.56-21.58 percent at the start of November.
